In a nutshell
I read your note. I am not convinced. Everywhere I have worked, people leave for money and then tell you it was something else.
That is often true. What the data says here is something narrower. It is the people under a year of service we are losing, and their pay is at the market rate.
At the rate you benchmarked. Benchmarks lag. A competitor can move in March and the survey shows it in September.

Agreed, and that is a fair caveat. Let me spell out why I still think it is not pay. The leavers with three years or more are on the same benchmark and they are not going anywhere. Same pay, different behaviour.
Hm. So what are you actually asking for?
What I am asking for is one owner for onboarding at each site. Not a new process and not more budget. The trade-off is that Ana comes off the engagement survey until December.
That I can live with. And if attrition has not moved by December?
Then I was wrong and we look at pay properly, with a survey we commission ourselves. In a nutshell, give me one quarter and one person.

It is the first ninety days that we are losing people in, not the pay.

Almost everybody who comes to me thinks the problem is their voice. It is not their voice. It is the order of the sentence. Here is what a nervous speaker does. They put every condition first, and by the time the point arrives, forty seconds have gone and nobody knows what they are being asked. Given the constraints and the timeline and the feedback from the sites, we might possibly consider looking at onboarding. What a confident speaker does is the reverse. What I need is one owner for onboarding. Then, and only then, the conditions. Same information, same words, different order, completely different room. And the second thing I fix is the ending. Do not trail off. Do not add so, yeah, at the end. Say the last word and then close your mouth. The silence is not awkward, the silence is the point landing.

I have been talked out of a position exactly twice in fifteen years, and both times it was done the same way. The person agreed with my objection first. Not politely, actually agreed, and said which part of it was right. That did something to me. I stopped preparing my next sentence and started listening, because I was no longer being resisted. Then she said, here is the part where I still think you are wrong, and gave me one fact. One. Not five. And the fact was checkable, which meant I could not argue with it without going and looking, and I was not going to go and look in front of eight people. The third thing she did was tell me what she wanted before I had to ask. People think winning an argument is about pressure. It is about removing every reason the other person has to keep defending themselves.
